learnings.answer:
"Can it be rebranded per customer?" turns out to be an architectural question, not a styling one — and the answer is decided by choices you make long before anyone asks.

## The levels

| Level | What varies | Mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1 — Theming** | Colours, fonts, logo, radius | Semantic token swap at runtime |
| **2 — Branding** | The above plus copy, imagery, domain | Tokens + a content layer |
| **3 — Configuration** | Which features exist, which fields show | [Feature flags](/system-design/413) + a config-driven UI |
| **4 — Customisation** | Custom layouts, custom fields, custom workflows | A schema-driven renderer |
| **5 — Custom code** | Per-tenant components | Plugin architecture — very expensive |

Most products need 1–3 and accidentally build toward 5. Naming the level you are designing for is the first move.

## Level 1–2: tokens, resolved at runtime

```css
/* One stylesheet ships. The values arrive per tenant. */
:root {
  --color-brand: #2563eb;
  --color-brand-fg: #ffffff;
  --font-display: 'Inter', system-ui, sans-serif;
  --radius-control: 6px;
}
```

```javascript
// Applied before first paint, so there is no flash of the default brand.
const tenant = await fetch(`/api/tenants/${host}/theme`).then((r) => r.json());
for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(tenant.tokens)) {
  document.documentElement.style.setProperty(`--${key}`, value);
}
```

Two rules make this work, and both are decided early:

1. **No component may reference a raw value** — only semantic tokens. One `#2563eb` inside a component is a component that cannot be re-themed.
2. **Resolve the theme before first paint.** Server-render the token block into the HTML, or inline a tiny blocking script. Otherwise every tenant sees your default brand flash first, which is exactly what they are paying you not to happen.

### Contrast is a correctness problem

A tenant picks a pale yellow brand colour. Your white-on-brand button is now unreadable and you have shipped an accessibility failure to one customer.

```javascript
// Derive the foreground rather than letting the tenant choose it.
const fg = contrastRatio(brand, "#fff") >= 4.5 ? "#fff" : "#111";
```

Validate tenant tokens at the point they are set, and reject or auto-correct combinations that fail AA. This is not gold-plating; it is the difference between a theming feature and a per-tenant bug generator.

## Level 3: configuration

```javascript
// The tenant's capability set, resolved once and read everywhere.
const { features, fields } = useTenantConfig();

{
  features.exportCsv && <ExportButton />;
}
{
  fields.filter((f) => f.visible).map((f) => <Field key={f.id} {...f} />);
}
```

The discipline that keeps this maintainable: **the default is always "on" or always "off", consistently, and every flag has an owner and an expiry.** Flags without expiry dates are how a codebase acquires forty permanent branches nobody dares delete.

## Isolation — the part that is a security question

| Concern | The requirement |
| --- | --- |
| **Data** | The server enforces the tenant boundary. A client-side tenant id in a request is a suggestion, not a control. |
| **Cache keys** | Every cache key includes the tenant. Otherwise tenant A's data is served to tenant B — and that is a reportable breach. |
| **Storage** | `localStorage` and [IndexedDB](/web-fundamentals/16) are per-origin, not per-tenant. On a shared domain, namespace every key by tenant and clear on switch. |
| **[CDN](/system-design/115)** | Never cache a tenant-specific response publicly. `Vary` on the tenant, or keep it private. |
| **Error tracking** | Tag by tenant so you can tell "broken for everyone" from "broken for one customer". |

> "The riskiest part isn't the theming, it's the cache keys. If the tenant isn't in the key — in React Query, in the [service worker](/web-fundamentals/15), in the CDN — you will eventually serve one customer's data to another. I'd make the tenant part of the key by construction, not by convention."

## Routing per tenant

| Shape | Example | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Subdomain | `acme.app.com` | Clean isolation; wildcard TLS; separate storage origins **(the safest)** |
| Path | `app.com/acme` | Simplest; shared origin means shared storage — namespace carefully |
| Custom domain | `portal.acme.com` | What enterprise customers actually want; you now own certificate provisioning |

## Common mistakes

- **Hard-coded values in components.** Themability is now a rewrite.
- **Theme applied after hydration.** Every tenant sees your brand first.
- **Letting tenants pick both foreground and background.** You have outsourced your contrast compliance.
- **Tenant id missing from a cache key.** Cross-tenant data leak.
- **Flags with no expiry.** Permanent branching, untestable combinations.
- **Trusting a client-supplied tenant id.** The server must enforce it.

## Key takeaways

- Decide the level: token theming, branding, configuration, schema-driven, or plugins.
- Semantic tokens only, resolved before first paint.
- Derive foreground colours and validate contrast — tenant input is untrusted design input.
- Tenant identity belongs in every cache key, everywhere, or you will leak data across tenants.
- The server enforces the tenant boundary; the client only displays it.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"A tenant wants a different layout on one page."** — That is level 4. Either a schema-driven renderer or a documented slot in that page — not a per-tenant branch in the component.
- **"How do you prevent one tenant's data reaching another?"** — Server-side enforcement, plus the tenant in every cache key at every layer. Say all the layers.
- **"How do you test 40 tenants?"** — Test the mechanism against a few representative token sets, plus automated contrast validation on every tenant's configuration.

learnings.title: Observability — knowing it broke before the user tells you
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum

summary.definition: Observability is knowing your app broke before a user tells you. Backends get it by default; the frontend runs on devices you will never see, so every signal you get is one you deliberately shipped code to collect.

api.note: the two global hooks; without the second, every rejected promise is invisible

api.signature: source maps uploaded to the collector
api.note: or every stack is `a.min.js:1:48291` and useless
where you put them decides whether one widget fails or the whole page does
the field half of your performance metrics, from real devices
propagate it on fetch so a slow request links to the backend trace
how the data actually leaves — a normal fetch on page hide is often cancelled

summary.useCase: A checkout bug affecting only Safari 16 that nobody reported for a week — a grouped error with a readable stack would have surfaced it in an hour.

learnings.answer:
Backends get observability by default: logs, metrics, traces, all on machines you own. The frontend runs on devices you will never see, and unless you deliberately build a way to hear from them, your only monitoring is a support ticket.

Naming this in a design round is a cheap, reliable senior signal.

## The four signals

| Signal | Answers | Tools |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **RUM** | Is it fast for real people? | `web-vitals` → your own endpoint, CrUX, SpeedCurve |
| **Errors** | Is it broken, and where? | Sentry, Rollbar, Bugsnag |
| **Product analytics** | Did they succeed at the task? | Amplitude, PostHog, Mixpanel |
| **Session replay** | *Why* did it break? | Sentry Replay, FullStory, LogRocket |

You need all four because each answers a question the others cannot. Vitals say the page was fast; errors say nothing threw; and the user still could not check out.

## Errors, made actionable

Raw error counts are noise. Three things turn them into something you can act on:

```javascript
Sentry.init({
  dsn: process.env.SENTRY_DSN,
  release: __BUILD_SHA__, // 1. which deploy introduced it
  environment: __ENV__,
  tracesSampleRate: 0.1,
  replaysOnErrorSampleRate: 1.0, // replay every session that errored
  beforeSend(event) {
    // 2. drop the noise that is not yours
    if (event.exception?.values?.[0]?.value?.includes("ResizeObserver loop"))
      return null;
    if (isBrowserExtensionFrame(event)) return null;
    return event;
  },
});

// 3. who and where — without shipping personal data
Sentry.setUser({ id: user.id }); // an id, never an email
Sentry.setTag("tenant", tenant.id);
Sentry.setTag("route", location.pathname);
```

**Source maps are the difference between usable and useless.** Upload them at build time and do not serve them publicly — an error in `a.min.js:1:48291` tells you nothing.

### Error boundaries decide the blast radius

```javascript
// One boundary per major region. A crashed chart should not
// take the navigation with it.
<ErrorBoundary fallback={<ChartFailed onRetry={refetch} />}>
  <RevenueChart />
</ErrorBoundary>;
```

Where you place boundaries is an architectural decision: it determines whether a bug degrades one panel or blanks the page. Note that boundaries do **not** catch errors in event handlers, in async code, or during SSR — those need `window.onerror`, `unhandledrejection`, and server-side handling respectively.

## Tracing across the boundary

The highest-value and least-implemented piece. Propagate a trace id from the browser into the backend so one user's slow request is one timeline, not two disconnected investigations:

```javascript
const traceId = crypto.randomUUID();
fetch("/api/feed", { headers: { traceparent: `00-${traceId}-${spanId}-01` } });
```

> "I'd propagate W3C trace context from the client. Without it, 'the feed is slow for this customer' is two separate investigations that never meet in the middle."

## Sampling and volume

You cannot send everything from every session; the beacon traffic becomes its own problem.

| Data | Sample |
| --- | --- |
| Web vitals | 100% — they are tiny and you need the p75 |
| Errors | 100%, with aggressive deduplication server-side |
| Traces | 1–10%, plus 100% of anything that errored |
| Session replay | ~1% baseline, 100% on error |
| Custom events | 100% for funnel steps, sample the chatter |

Always use `navigator.sendBeacon` for telemetry on unload — `fetch` is routinely cancelled when the page goes away, which silently biases your data toward sessions that did not leave.

## Privacy is a design constraint

- **No PII in error payloads.** User ids, never emails or names. Scrub URLs with tokens in them.
- **Mask inputs in session replay by default**, and opt specific fields *in*, never out.
- **Telemetry is usually "non-essential"** under GDPR, so it waits for consent — which means it cannot be on your critical path anyway.
- **Data residency** may dictate which vendor and region you may use at all.

## Alerting on what users feel

Alert on symptoms, not causes:

| Alert | Threshold |
| --- | --- |
| JS error rate | > 2× the 7-day baseline for 10 min |
| p75 LCP | > 2.5 s on a key route for 15 min |
| API failure rate | > 1% on a critical endpoint |
| Checkout funnel drop | > 20% below the same hour last week |

That last one catches the class of bug nothing else does: **no errors, good vitals, and the button silently does nothing.**

## Common mistakes

- **Errors with no release tag.** You cannot tell which deploy caused it.
- **No source maps.** Minified stack traces are unreadable.
- **One error boundary at the root.** Any bug blanks the whole app.
- **Sending PII to a third party.** A compliance incident with your name on it.
- **`fetch` for unload beacons.** Cancelled, and your data quietly skews.
- **Vitals without funnels.** Fast and broken looks healthy on every dashboard.

## Key takeaways

- Four signals — RUM, errors, analytics, replay — because each answers a different question.
- Tag every event with release, route and tenant, or it is not actionable.
- [Error boundaries](/react-guide/25) per region decide the blast radius of a bug.
- Propagate W3C trace context so client and server slowness is one timeline.
- Alert on user-visible symptoms, including funnel drops that throw no errors.
- `sendBeacon`, never `fetch`, for anything sent on unload.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"How do you know a deploy made things worse?"** — Release-tagged vitals and error rates, compared against the previous release on the same routes, during the [canary](/system-design/114).
- **"A user says it's broken and you can't reproduce it."** — Session replay filtered to their user id, plus the trace id from their request.
- **"How much does this cost?"** — Sampling is the lever: 100% vitals and errors, 1–10% traces, 1% replay with 100% on error.

learnings.title: Containers for frontend engineers — what Docker actually does
learnings.source: user request: Docker and Kubernetes for frontend system design

summary.definition: Docker packages your app and everything it needs to run into one image that behaves the same on any machine. For a frontend the interesting question is not Docker itself — it is what happens to your build output after CI goes green.

api.note: build with Node, copy only `dist/` into a tiny serving image — not the whole toolchain
layer ordering: dependencies cache, so a source change does not reinstall them
keep `node_modules`, `.git` and `.env` out of the build context entirely
the frontend trap — `VITE_*` is baked in at build, so one image cannot serve two environments
an image built on an Apple laptop will not run on an x86 node unless you say so
for the local loop — the app plus its API and database in one command

summary.useCase: One image promoted from staging to production, where the API URL is read at runtime — because baking it in at build time means rebuilding to deploy the same code.

learnings.answer:
You are not being interviewed on Docker. You are being interviewed on what happens to your build output after CI goes green, and "we containerise it" is the answer that gets followed up on. This is the amount of Docker that survives those follow-ups.

## The three words, precisely

| Word | What it is | The analogy that is close enough |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Image** | A read-only, layered filesystem plus a start command | The build artefact — a `.zip` of a whole machine |
| **Container** | One running instance of an image, isolated by the kernel | The process — you can run twenty from one image |
| **Registry** | Where images are pushed and pulled from | npm, but for images (ECR, GCR, Docker Hub) |

A container is **not a VM**. There is no guest kernel; it is your host's kernel with the process fenced off by namespaces and cgroups. That is why it starts in milliseconds and why "it works on my machine" only mostly goes away — the kernel and the CPU architecture are still shared, which is exactly why an M-series Mac builds an `arm64` image that a cluster of `amd64` nodes cannot run.

## The multi-stage build

The single most important idea, and the one interviewers actually check for: **the image that builds your app and the image that runs it are different images**.

![Multi-stage build — the toolchain does not ship](/diagrams/sysdesign/container-anatomy.svg)

For a static SPA, the runtime is a web server, not Node:

```dockerfile
# ---- Stage 1: build ----
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app

# Dependencies first, in their own layer. This is the whole trick — see below.
COPY package.json pnpm-lock.yaml ./
RUN corepack enable && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

COPY . .
RUN pnpm build          # -> /app/dist

# ---- Stage 2: run ----
FROM nginx:1.27-alpine
COPY --from=builder /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html
COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
EXPOSE 8080
```

Everything in stage 1 — source, `node_modules`, the toolchain — is discarded. What ships is nginx plus your `dist/`: roughly 25 MB instead of 1.2 GB. That matters for more than tidiness: the image is pulled on every scale-up and every node replacement, and a 1.2 GB pull is a slow autoscale during exactly the traffic spike that triggered it.

The nginx config has to know two frontend things — SPA fallback and the caching split from **[Build and deploy topology](/system-design/109)**:

```text
server {
  listen 8080;
  root /usr/share/nginx/html;

  # Hashed assets: cache forever.
  location /assets/ {
    add_header Cache-Control "public, max-age=31536000, immutable";
  }

  # The HTML is the manifest. Never cache it.
  location / {
    add_header Cache-Control "no-cache";
    try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html;   # SPA deep links
  }
}
```

For an SSR app there is no nginx — the runtime image is Node, and the only rule is that it must not carry the build toolchain or dev dependencies:

```dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json pnpm-lock.yaml ./
RUN corepack enable && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
COPY . .
RUN pnpm build

FROM node:20-alpine AS runner
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY --from=builder /app/.next/standalone ./
COPY --from=builder /app/.next/static ./.next/static
COPY --from=builder /app/public ./public

# Do not run as root. A container escape should not land on a root shell.
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

## Layers, and why the order of two lines changes your CI time

An image is a stack of layers, one per instruction. Docker caches each layer and reuses it while its inputs are unchanged — **but a changed layer invalidates every layer after it**.

```dockerfile
# Slow: every source edit re-runs the install.
COPY . .
RUN pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

# Fast: the install layer only rebuilds when the lockfile changes.
COPY package.json pnpm-lock.yaml ./
RUN pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
COPY . .
```

Same two instructions, opposite order. The first re-downloads your entire dependency tree on every commit — a 90-second penalty per CI run, per developer, forever. The second reuses it until someone actually changes a dependency.

The matching `.dockerignore` is not optional; without it `COPY . .` sends your `node_modules`, `.git` and local `.env` into the build context and into the image:

```text
node_modules
.git
dist
.env*
*.log
coverage
```

## Build-time vs runtime config — the frontend-specific trap

This is where frontend containers differ from backend ones, and it is worth saying out loud in an interview.

A backend reads `process.env` when it starts, so one image runs in every environment. A **[bundler](/web-fundamentals/9) inlines `import.meta.env.VITE_*` at build time** — the value becomes a string literal inside the JavaScript. So this:

```dockerfile
ARG VITE_API_URL          # ✗ now the image is environment-specific
RUN pnpm build
```

...produces one image per environment, which means staging never tested the artefact production runs, and a URL change requires a rebuild and a re-test. Two ways out:

```javascript
// Option A — fetch config at boot. Works for SPA and SSR, no image rebuild.
const config = await fetch("/config.json", { cache: "no-store" }).then((r) =>
  r.json(),
);

// /config.json is mounted into the container from a ConfigMap,
// so the same image is promoted from staging to production untouched.
```

```bash
# Option B — substitute placeholders at container start, before nginx boots.
# docker-entrypoint.sh
envsubst '${API_URL}' < /usr/share/nginx/html/config.template.js \
  > /usr/share/nginx/html/config.js
exec nginx -g 'daemon off;'
```

Either is fine. Baking the value in is what loses the point.

> "I'd keep environment out of the image entirely — build one artefact, mount config at runtime. Otherwise 'we tested it in staging' is not true, because staging ran a different binary."

## Compose, for the local loop

`docker compose` is the local-development half of this. It matters in an interview only as the answer to "how does a new engineer run the stack" — but that question does get asked.

```yaml
services:
  web:
    build: { context: ., target: builder }
    command: pnpm dev --host
    ports: ['5173:5173']
    volumes:
      - .:/app                 # your edits, live
      - /app/node_modules      # keep the container's, not the host's
    environment:
      - VITE_API_URL=http://localhost:4000

  bff:
    build: ./bff
    ports: ['4000:4000']
    depends_on: [db]

  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: dev }
```

The anonymous volume on `node_modules` is the line everyone gets wrong: without it, your host's `node_modules` (built on macOS/arm64) shadows the container's, and native modules break in a way that takes an afternoon to diagnose.

## What a container does not solve

- **It is not a [CDN](/system-design/115).** Serving your hashed assets from nginx inside a pod means every asset request crosses the ingress and burns pod CPU. Assets belong in object storage behind a CDN; the container serves the HTML and the API.
- **It is not a bundler.** A 900 kB main chunk is 900 kB whether or not it is in a container.
- **It is not isolation from your dependencies.** A malicious postinstall script runs during your build, inside the builder stage, with network access.

## Common mistakes

- **A single-stage image**, shipping node, the source and the dev dependencies to production.
- **`COPY . .` before the install**, throwing away the dependency layer cache on every commit.
- **No `.dockerignore`**, so the build context includes `node_modules`, `.git` and `.env`.
- **Baking `VITE_*` into the image**, which forces one image per environment.
- **Running as root**, because the base image defaults to it and nobody changed it.
- **`FROM node:latest`**, so a rebuild in three months is a different base image and a mystery failure.
- **Serving assets from the pod** instead of the CDN.

## Key takeaways

- Multi-stage: build in a fat image, run in a thin one. The toolchain never ships.
- Copy the lockfile and install before copying source — layer order is your CI time.
- Pin the base image tag, run as a non-root user, and keep the runtime image boring.
- Config is mounted or fetched at runtime, never baked in — one artefact, promoted.
- The container is the unit of *deployment*, not a substitute for a CDN or a budget.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"Why not just one stage?"** — Because the runtime would carry the compiler, the source and every dev dependency: a slower pull on each scale-up and a much larger attack surface, for zero runtime benefit.
- **"Your image is 1.4 GB. Where did it go wrong?"** — Almost always a single-stage build, or `COPY . .` with no `.dockerignore` dragging in `node_modules` and `.git`.
- **"How do you run the same build in three environments?"** — One image, promoted. Config comes from a mounted `config.json` or an entrypoint substitution, so staging and production run identical bytes.
- **"CI takes eleven minutes to build the image."** — Check layer order first, then the base image and the build context size; a dependency layer that never gets a cache hit is usually the whole gap.

learnings.title: Kubernetes for frontend engineers — the objects that matter
learnings.source: user request: Docker and Kubernetes for frontend system design

summary.definition: Kubernetes runs and restarts your containers across a pool of machines. Nobody expects a frontend candidate to operate a cluster; they expect you to know where your container runs, what routes traffic to it, and which failures are yours.

api.note: one or more containers running together — the thing that actually dies and gets replaced
declares how many pods you want and handles the rollout when the image changes
a stable address in front of pods whose ip addresses keep changing
routes by host and path from outside — where `/api/*` and `/assets/*` diverge
the one that matters: fail it and you are taken out of rotation instead of serving errors
requests get you scheduled; exceeding a memory limit gets you `OOMKilled`

summary.useCase: A rollout that serves 502s for thirty seconds because the readiness probe passed before the server could actually answer.

learnings.answer:
Nobody expects a frontend candidate to operate a cluster. They expect you to know **where your container runs, what routes traffic to it, and what you are responsible for** — because the alternative answer is "it goes to the DevOps team", and that ends the conversation. Five objects carry ninety percent of it. ## The request path ![Kubernetes for a frontend — the objects on the request path](/diagrams/sysdesign/k8s-request-path.svg) The sentence to lead with: **most of your traffic should never reach a pod.** Hashed assets are immutable and belong on a [CDN](/system-design/115) in front of object storage. What reaches the cluster is the HTML document and the API calls — and if that is not true, you are paying pod CPU and ingress bandwidth to serve files that a CDN would serve for free from a city closer to the user. ## The five objects | Object | What it does | What you write | | --- | --- | --- | | **Pod** | One or more containers scheduled together, sharing an IP. The unit that runs. | Rarely by hand | | **Deployment** | The desired state — this image, this many replicas — and the controller that rolls it out. Creates a ReplicaSet, which creates Pods. | Yes | | **Service** | A stable DNS name and virtual IP in front of a set of pods, matched by label. Pods die and get new IPs; the Service name does not change. | Yes | | **Ingress** | The HTTP entrance: TLS termination, host and path routing, traffic weights. | Yes, or your platform does | | **ConfigMap / Secret** | Key-value config, mounted as files or env vars at runtime. Secrets are the same thing with tighter access and (hopefully) encryption at rest. | Yes | A Deployment for a frontend, with everything that matters and nothing that does not: ```yaml apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: web spec: replicas: 3 selector: matchLabels: { app: web } template: metadata: labels: { app: web } spec: containers: - name: web image: registry.example.com/web:2f9c1a4 # a digest or a SHA tag, never :latest ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }] envFrom: - configMapRef: { name: web-config } # runtime config, same image everywhere resources: requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 256Mi } # what the scheduler reserves limits: { cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi } # where it gets throttled / killed readinessProbe: httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 } periodSeconds: 5 livenessProbe: httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 } initialDelaySeconds: 30 ``` And the two objects that put it on the internet: ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: web spec: selector: { app: web } # matches the pod labels above — this is the whole binding ports: [{ port: 80, targetPort: 8080 }] --- apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: Ingress metadata: name: web spec: tls: [{ hosts: [app.example.com], secretName: web-tls }] rules: - host: app.example.com http: paths: - path: /api pathType: Prefix backend: { service: { name: bff, port: { number: 80 } } } - path: / pathType: Prefix backend: { service: { name: web, port: { number: 80 } } } ``` Read the binding out loud once and it stops being mysterious: the Deployment stamps pods with `app: web`, the Service selects that label, the Ingress points at the Service. **Labels are the wiring** — a typo in one of them is the classic "my Service returns 503 and everything looks fine". ## Probes — the one that actually matters is readiness | Probe | Fails → what happens | Use it for | | --- | --- | --- | | `startupProbe` | Nothing yet; it just holds the other two off | A slow boot (a big SSR warm-up) | | `readinessProbe` | The Service stops routing traffic here. The pod keeps running. | "Am I able to serve right now?" | | `livenessProbe` | The container is **killed and restarted** | "Am I wedged and unrecoverable?" | Readiness is what makes a rollout safe: a new pod receives no traffic until it says it is ready, and a pod that goes unhealthy is quietly taken out of rotation instead of returning errors. Two failure modes worth being able to describe: - **No readiness probe.** The rollout considers a pod ready the instant the process starts, and sends real users to a Node server that has not finished loading its render bundle. You see a burst of 502s on every deploy. - **A liveness probe pointed at something slow.** The app takes 40 s to boot, liveness fires at 30 s, the container is killed, and it restarts forever — a `CrashLoopBackOff` that is not a crash at all. That is what `startupProbe` exists for. Make `/healthz` cheap and honest: it should not call the database, and it should return non-200 while the process genuinely cannot serve. ## Requests, limits, and autoscaling - **`requests`** is what the scheduler reserves — it decides which node you land on. - **`limits`** is the ceiling. Exceed the CPU limit and you are throttled; exceed the memory limit and the container is **OOMKilled** with no stack trace, which for an SSR pod usually means a render leak or a limit set below the Node heap. ```yaml apiVersion: autoscaling/v2 kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler metadata: { name: web } spec: scaleTargetRef: { apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: web } minReplicas: 3 maxReplicas: 20 metrics: - type: Resource resource: { name: cpu, target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 60 } } ``` For a **static SPA** pod this is nearly pointless — nginx serving files is not CPU-bound and the CDN absorbs the traffic anyway. For an **SSR pod** it is the main lever, because rendering is CPU work and one slow render blocks the [event loop](/learnings/128). Scale SSR on CPU, and remember that autoscaling has a lag: pods take time to pull, boot and pass readiness, so a spike is absorbed by headroom, not by the HPA. ## The five commands you should be able to say ```bash kubectl get pods -l app=web # is it running, how many restarts kubectl logs -f deploy/web # stdout — your app's logs, if you log to stdout kubectl describe pod web-7f9c-xyz # events: image pull errors, OOMKilled, probe failures kubectl rollout status deploy/web # is the deploy finished, or stuck kubectl port-forward svc/web 8080:80 # hit the Service from your laptop, bypassing the CDN ``` `describe` is the one that answers "why is it not starting" nine times out of ten: the Events list at the bottom names the image pull failure, the failed probe or the OOMKill directly. ## Where the frontend concerns actually land ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Hashed assets
immutable"] --> CDN["CDN + object storage"] B["HTML document"] --> ING["Ingress"] C["/api/*"] --> ING ING --> SVC["Service"] --> POD["Pods (SSR / BFF)"] POD --> UP["Upstream APIs"] ``` - **Assets** never touch the cluster. Upload them at build time; the pod does not own them. - **HTML** is either a file (SPA) or a render (SSR). Only the second one needs pods that scale. - **`/api/*`** goes to your [BFF](/system-design/102), usually its own Deployment, so it can scale separately from rendering. - **Config** arrives from a ConfigMap so one image serves every environment. ## Common mistakes - **`image: myapp:latest`.** Kubernetes cannot tell that the image changed, rollbacks are meaningless, and two pods can silently run different code. Use the commit SHA or a digest. - **No readiness probe**, so every deploy has an error spike. - **Liveness where readiness belonged**, turning slow boots into a restart loop. - **Memory limit below the Node heap**, giving OOMKills that look like random crashes. - **Serving `/assets/*` from the pod**, paying pod CPU for what a CDN does for free. - **Config baked into the image**, so "promote the artefact" becomes "rebuild per environment". - **Reciting object names without the request path.** Anyone can list Pod/Service/Ingress; the signal is knowing what stops at the CDN. ## Key takeaways - Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pod; Service gives them a stable name; Ingress is the door; ConfigMap/Secret is the environment. Labels wire them together. - Static assets belong on a CDN, not in a pod. That single sentence is most of the frontend answer. - Readiness makes rollouts safe; liveness restarts wedged containers; startup covers slow boots. - Requests schedule you, limits kill you. Watch memory on SSR pods. - Scale SSR on CPU, and give the HPA headroom because pods are not instant. - You are a consumer of this platform: what you owe it is a small image, an honest `/healthz`, and config read at runtime. ## Interview follow-ups - **"Where do your static assets live?"** — Object storage behind a CDN, uploaded at build time, hashed and immutable. The pods serve the document and the API only. - **"A pod is `CrashLoopBackOff`. Where do you look?"** — `kubectl describe` for the events, then `logs --previous`. Usually an OOMKill, a failing liveness probe on a slow boot, or a missing ConfigMap key. - **"Why three replicas and not one?"** — A node can vanish; a rollout needs somewhere to send traffic; and one pod means one event loop for every render. - **"How does a request reach your code?"** — DNS → CDN (assets stop here) → Ingress, which terminates TLS and routes by host and path → Service → one pod. - **"What would you scale on?"** — CPU for SSR, because rendering is CPU-bound. For a static SPA the honest answer is that you barely scale the pods at all; the CDN is the scaling story.

learnings.title: Running SSR on Kubernetes — rollouts, probes and the stale-chunk trap
learnings.source: user request: Docker and Kubernetes for frontend system design

summary.definition: A static SPA barely needs a cluster — it is files, and a CDN serves files. The moment you render on the server you own a long-lived Node process, per request, under a rollout — which brings memory limits, graceful shutdown and the stale-chunk problem.

api.signature: SIGTERM → stop accepting, finish in flight
api.note: graceful shutdown; without it a rollout drops requests mid-render
how long you get before `SIGKILL` — longer than your slowest render
an old tab asks for `/assets/feed.a1b2c3.js` and the new pods have never heard of it
the fix: detect the new build and prompt a reload rather than 404ing
how much old and new run together — and therefore how long both asset sets must exist
set below the container limit, or Node grows into `OOMKilled` rather than garbage collecting

summary.useCase: Users on an open tab getting a white screen after every deploy, because their lazy-loaded chunk no longer exists on the new pods.

learnings.answer:
A static SPA barely needs a cluster: it is files, and a CDN serves files. The moment you render on the server you own **a long-lived Node process, per user request, under a memory limit** — and that is a different job. This entry is the part of the deploy story an interviewer pushes into once you have said "we run Next.js in [Kubernetes](/system-design/113)".

## Why SSR changes the shape

| | Static SPA | SSR / [BFF](/system-design/102) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What the pod serves | Files (and ideally not even that — the CDN does) | A render per request, on the [event loop](/learnings/128) |
| Scaling signal | Barely scales; the CDN absorbs traffic | CPU — rendering is CPU-bound |
| A slow request costs | Nothing else | Every other request on that pod's event loop |
| Memory | Flat | Grows with concurrency, caches and leaks |
| Cold start | None | Seconds — module load, warm-up, first render |
| Deploy risk | A bad file | A bad process: leaks, restarts, dropped in-flight renders |

The one-liner: **an SPA pod is stateless and cheap; an SSR pod is a stateful-ish, CPU-bound server that just happens to emit HTML.**

## The rollout, and what the browser feels

![Rolling, blue-green, canary — what the browser experiences](/diagrams/sysdesign/rollout-strategies.svg)

All three put two versions in front of users at once. That is not a bug to be engineered away — it is the condition you design for.

| Strategy | Cost | Rollback | Pick it when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Rolling** | Cheapest; both versions serve for a minute or two | Roll forward, or re-deploy the old image | Default, low-stakes changes |
| **Blue / green** | Double the pods while both are up | One selector flip — seconds | Rollback speed is the requirement |
| **Canary** | Needs traffic splitting and real metrics | Drop the canary weight to zero | A regression must be caught on 1% of users |

Canary is the one that scores, because the interesting half is the **stop rule**: what metric, measured over what window, aborts the ramp. For a frontend, error rate is not enough — a deploy that doubles LCP or [INP](/system-design/401) is an incident that never throws.

```yaml
# Canary as an ingress weight — 5% of traffic to the new Deployment.
metadata:
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary: 'true'
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-weight: '5'
```

```yaml
# Rolling, tuned so capacity never dips during the roll.
spec:
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1          # one extra pod above the replica count
      maxUnavailable: 0    # never go below it — no capacity dip
```

## The failure that is actually yours: stale chunks

A user has had the tab open for twenty minutes. They click a lazily-loaded route. The browser requests `/assets/feed.a1b2c3.js` — a filename that only existed in v1. Every v1 pod is gone. **404, an unhandled dynamic-import rejection, a blank screen, and their half-written form.**

This is the same hazard as in **[Build and deploy topology](/system-design/109)**, and orchestration makes it worse: a rolling update deletes the old pods, and with them any file that only lived inside them.

Three mitigations, and you want all three:

1. **Assets are not pod resources.** Upload the hashed files to object storage at build time and serve them from the CDN. Retiring a pod then removes nothing the browser can still ask for.
2. **Keep the last few builds.** Storage is cheap; a broken session is not. Retain three or four.
3. **Tell the tab.** Poll a tiny `/version.json`, and when the build SHA changes, offer a reload — never force one.

```javascript
// A dynamic import that fails after a deploy should ask, not explode.
const load = (fn) =>
  fn().catch(async (err) => {
    const { build } = await fetch("/version.json", { cache: "no-store" }).then(
      (r) => r.json(),
    );
    if (build !== __BUILD_SHA__) {
      showToast("A new version is available", {
        action: "Reload",
        onAction: () => location.reload(),
      });
      return { default: () => null };
    }
    throw err;
  });

const Feed = lazy(() => load(() => import("./routes/Feed")));
```

## Graceful shutdown — the other half of a clean rollout

When Kubernetes retires a pod it sends `SIGTERM`, waits `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`, then `SIGKILL`s it. A Node server that exits immediately on `SIGTERM` **drops every in-flight response** — and for streaming SSR that is a half-written HTML document in someone's browser.

```yaml
lifecycle:
  preStop:
    exec:
      # Let the endpoint removal propagate before we stop accepting work.
      command: ['sh', '-c', 'sleep 5']
terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
```

```javascript
// Stop taking new work, finish what is open, then exit.
process.on("SIGTERM", () => {
  isShuttingDown = true; // /healthz now returns 503, so readiness pulls us from the Service
  server.close(() => process.exit(0));
  setTimeout(() => process.exit(1), 25_000).unref(); // never hang past the grace period
});
```

The `preStop` sleep looks like a hack and is not: endpoint removal and the `SIGTERM` race each other, so without it a few requests are routed to a pod that has already begun shutting down.

## No sticky sessions, so no in-process state

A user's next request lands on a different pod. Everything that follows from that:

- **In-memory session state is a bug.** It is in one pod's heap; the next request misses it.
- **An in-process render cache is a warm cache, never a source of truth.** Ten pods mean ten cold caches and ten times the origin load on a deploy. Put the shared cache in Redis, or at the CDN.
- **Rate limiting and feature-flag state need a shared store**, or each pod enforces its own tenth of the limit.
- **Do not reach for sticky sessions to fix this.** They make rollouts and autoscaling worse, and they hide the actual bug.

## Memory, cold start, and the numbers to have ready

- **Set the Node heap under the container limit.** `--max-old-space-size=768` inside a 1 Gi limit; the process also uses memory outside the heap, and a limit equal to the heap is an OOMKill waiting for traffic.
- **An OOMKill has no stack trace.** `kubectl describe pod` shows `Reason: OOMKilled` and nothing else. Slow, repeated OOMKills usually mean a per-render leak — a module-scope array, a cache with no bound.
- **Cold start is seconds.** Module load, framework warm-up, first render. `startupProbe` covers it, and the HPA cannot: by the time a new pod is ready the spike has arrived. Carry headroom.
- **Rough figures you can reason with:** an SSR render is single-digit to tens of milliseconds of CPU; a pod with 1 CPU handles order-of tens of renders per second; anything cacheable at the CDN should never become a render at all.

> "Before scaling the pods I'd check how much of that traffic needs a render at all. Most SSR capacity problems are a caching problem wearing a scaling costume."

## Common mistakes

- **Serving hashed assets from the SSR pod**, so a rollout deletes files that open tabs still request.
- **`maxUnavailable` left at its default** during a rollout that removes capacity right when the new pods are still warming.
- **No `SIGTERM` handling**, so every rollout drops in-flight renders.
- **In-memory sessions or a cache treated as authoritative** across replicas.
- **Memory limit set to the heap size**, then blaming Kubernetes for the OOMKills.
- **Canary with no stop rule**, or one that watches 500s and ignores vitals.
- **Autoscaling as the answer to a spike**, when the pods take 40 seconds to become ready.

## Key takeaways

- SSR pods are CPU-bound servers; SPAs are files. Only one of them really needs the cluster.
- Every rollout runs two versions at once. Assets on the CDN and a version check are what make that survivable.
- `maxSurge` / `maxUnavailable` decide whether capacity dips mid-deploy; `SIGTERM` handling decides whether in-flight renders survive it.
- No sticky sessions: shared state goes in a shared store, and in-process caches are warm caches only.
- Keep the Node heap under the container limit, and expect cold start to outlast the traffic spike.
- Canary is only a strategy if it has a stop rule, and for a frontend that rule includes [Core Web Vitals](/system-design/402).

## Interview follow-ups

- **"You deploy while a user has the tab open. What breaks?"** — A lazy chunk 404s if assets lived in the pod. Fixed by CDN-hosted assets, retaining old builds, and a version check that offers a reload.
- **"Rolling or blue-green here?"** — Whichever matches the cost of a bad version: rolling for cheap and low-stakes, blue-green when rollback must take seconds, canary when the regression must be found before everyone has it.
- **"How do you know the canary is healthy?"** — Error rate, plus LCP/INP on the canary cohort, over a window long enough to be real traffic. A vitals regression is a rollback trigger.
- **"Your SSR pods are OOMKilled twice a day."** — Heap limit versus container limit first, then a heap snapshot for a per-render retain; module-scope caches with no bound are the usual culprit.
- **"Why not cache the render in the pod?"** — Ten pods, ten cold caches, and the hit rate collapses after every deploy. Shared cache or CDN, with the pod cache as a bonus.

learnings.title: CDN and the edge — cache keys, invalidation, origin shielding
learnings.source: user request: senior frontend networking — CDN, HTTP protocols, edge

summary.definition: A CDN is a network of servers near your users that hold copies of your responses. It is the largest single performance lever a frontend has, and the cache key — what makes two requests "the same" — is the part that decides whether it works at all.

api.note: usually host + path + query; a `?utm_source=` on the end makes it a different object entirely

summary.useCase: A cache hit rate of 3% traced to analytics query parameters — every share link was a unique cache key for identical content.

learnings.answer:
The CDN is the largest single performance lever a frontend has, and the one most often configured once and never understood. In an interview it is also where "and then we deploy it" turns into a real conversation.

![CDN and the edge](/diagrams/sysdesign/cdn-edge.svg)

## What it actually is

A network of PoPs — points of presence, a few hundred of them — each with a cache, sitting between the user and your origin. A request goes to the nearest PoP; on a hit it never travels further. That removes both halves of the latency problem: the distance ([the life of a request](/browser/160)) and the origin's work.

| Content | Where it should be served from |
| --- | --- |
| Hashed assets (`app.8f3a2b.js`) | Edge, `immutable`, forever |
| Images and video | Edge, transformed per device |
| HTML for anonymous users | Edge, short TTL or stale-while-revalidate |
| HTML for logged-in users | Origin, or edge with a user-aware cache key |
| `POST` / mutations | Origin, never cached |

## The cache key is the whole game

A CDN caches by a key it derives from the request. By default: host + path + query. Everything else you must configure deliberately, because each addition multiplies the number of cached copies.

- **Query strings.** Marketing parameters (`?utm_source=…`) are not content. If they are in the key, every campaign link is a separate cache entry and your hit rate collapses. Strip them.
- **`Vary`.** `Vary: Accept-Encoding` is necessary. `Vary: User-Agent` is a catastrophe — thousands of variants of the same file. Use a small normalised device class instead.
- **Cookies.** If any cookie is in the key, an analytics cookie makes every user unique. Configure the cache to ignore all cookies except the ones that genuinely change the response.

Hit rate is the metric. Below ~90% on static assets, the key is wrong.

## Two headers, two jobs

```http
# Hashed asset: the name changes when the content does.
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

# HTML: the manifest. Revalidate every time, but serve instantly meanwhile.
Cache-Control: public, max-age=0, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=600
```

- `max-age` is for the **browser**; `s-maxage` is for the **shared cache** (the CDN). They can and should differ: `max-age=0, s-maxage=60` means the browser always asks and the CDN answers most of those asks from RAM.
- `stale-while-revalidate` serves the stale copy instantly and refreshes in the background. It is the single highest-value header for HTML, and almost free.
- `stale-if-error` keeps you up when the origin is down.

Full detail on the browser side in [HTTP Caching](/browser/157).

## Invalidation

**Purging is the fallback, not the plan.** A global purge takes seconds to minutes to propagate and creates a thundering herd of misses against your origin at exactly the wrong moment.

1. **Versioned URLs** — the hashed filename. Nothing to invalidate: a new build is new URLs, and the old ones stay cached for the tabs still using them.
2. **Surrogate keys / cache tags** — tag responses (`product-42`), purge by tag when that thing changes. This is how you cache logged-out HTML safely.
3. **Short TTL + `stale-while-revalidate`** — for content that changes unpredictably and can be a minute stale.
4. **Explicit purge** — for the mistake you need gone now.

## Origin shielding and the herd

Without a shield, a cold cache in 200 PoPs means 200 origin requests for the same file. **Origin shield** designates one PoP as the origin's only client: every other PoP fetches through it, so your origin sees one request. Combined with **request coalescing** (the CDN collapses concurrent misses for the same key into one upstream fetch), that is what stops a purge from taking the origin down.

## What runs at the edge

Beyond caching, PoPs can execute code — routing, A/B assignment, auth checks, header rewriting, personalisation of an otherwise cached page. That is [edge functions](/system-design/116), and it is what makes "cache the HTML" viable for pages that are not identical for everyone.

## Common mistakes

- Caching the HTML with a long `max-age`, so a deploy never reaches anyone and the fix is behind the same cached HTML.
- Leaving query strings and cookies in the cache key, then wondering why the hit rate is 40%.
- `Vary: User-Agent`.
- Purging everything on every deploy instead of using hashed filenames.
- Serving assets from your pods rather than the CDN ([running SSR on Kubernetes](/system-design/114)).
- No `stale-if-error`, so an origin blip becomes a user-visible outage.

## Key takeaways

- The cache key decides the hit rate; strip marketing params, ignore irrelevant cookies, never vary on user-agent.
- `max-age` for the browser, `s-maxage` for the CDN, `stale-while-revalidate` for the experience.
- Invalidate by versioned URL or surrogate key; purge is the emergency lever.
- Origin shield plus request coalescing is what protects the origin from a cold cache.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"How do you cache HTML for logged-in users?"** — Usually you do not: cache the shell, personalise at the edge or on the client, and tag anything you do cache so it can be purged precisely.
- **"A deploy went out and users still see the old app."** — Cached HTML. Check `Cache-Control` on the document; the assets are hashed so they are not the problem.
- **"Your origin fell over right after a purge."** — Thundering herd. Origin shield, request coalescing, and staggered TTLs rather than one global expiry.

learnings.title: Edge functions — the runtime, the limits, and what belongs there
learnings.source: user request: senior frontend networking — CDN, HTTP protocols, edge

summary.definition: An edge function is code that runs inside the CDN's point of presence, between the user and your origin. It is not a smaller container — it is a different runtime with no filesystem, no Node APIs and a hard limit on how long it may run.

api.note: web APIs only — this is the whole surface you can rely on

api.signature: no fs, no net, no child_process
api.note: no Node built-ins, which rules out most npm packages outright
the canonical fit: A/B bucketing or geo routing, decided before the origin is touched
cheap at the edge, and they keep unauthenticated traffic off your origin entirely
what does not belong — your data is not at the edge, so you have added a hop
fast to start and billed per call — a bad fit for something on every asset request

summary.useCase: Bucketing users into an A/B variant at the edge and rewriting the path, so both variants stay fully cacheable instead of forcing every request to the origin.

learnings.answer:
An edge function is code that runs *in the [CDN](/system-design/115) PoP*, between the user and your origin. It is not a smaller container — it is a different runtime with different rules, and knowing those rules is the difference between a good answer and a buzzword.

## The runtime

Most edge platforms run V8 isolates, not Node processes: a few milliseconds to start, a few megabytes of memory, thousands per machine. What you give up in exchange:

| Available | Not available |
| --- | --- |
| `fetch`, `Request`, `Response`, `URL`, `Headers` | `fs`, `net`, `child_process`, most Node built-ins |
| Web Crypto, `TextEncoder`, streams | Native modules, long-lived TCP (so most database drivers) |
| KV / edge storage, per-request context | Local disk, in-process state between requests |
| CPU in the tens of milliseconds | Long-running work, heavy computation |

So an edge function talks HTTP, transforms requests and responses, and returns quickly. A dependency that imports `fs` at module load will not even boot — the usual first surprise.

## What belongs at the edge

- **Routing and rewrites** — geography, locale, device class, a legacy path map.
- **A/B assignment** — read or set the bucket cookie and rewrite to the right variant, before anything is cached. Doing this on the client is a flash of the wrong variant.
- **Auth gating** — verify a [JWT](/browser/158) signature and redirect or 401. Cheap, and it keeps unauthenticated traffic off the origin entirely.
- **Personalising a cached page** — serve one cached HTML for everyone and patch in the name, currency or [feature flags](/system-design/413) at the edge. This is what makes edge caching viable for signed-in users.
- **Headers and security** — [CSP](/system-design/407) nonces, HSTS, cache-control normalisation, stripping marketing params before they reach the cache key.
- **Geolocation** — the PoP already knows the country; the origin would have to guess from an IP.
- **Image transformation** — resize and re-encode per device at the edge, cache the variant.

## What does not

- **Anything with a database connection pool.** No long-lived TCP, and 300 PoPs opening connections to one primary is a bad idea even where the driver works. Use an HTTP data API, or keep it in the origin.
- **Heavy computation.** PDF generation, large renders, image processing beyond the platform's own primitives — CPU limits are tight and per-request.
- **Work that needs shared state.** Isolates are ephemeral and distributed; there is no in-process cache you can rely on and no ordering between PoPs.
- **Anything latency-insensitive.** If it does not need to be near the user, the edge only makes it harder to debug.

```javascript
// A/B assignment at the edge: one cached page per variant, no client-side flash.
export default async function middleware(request) {
  const url = new URL(request.url);
  const cookie = request.headers.get("cookie") ?? "";
  const existing = /(?:^|;\s*)bucket=(a|b)/.exec(cookie)?.[1];
  const bucket = existing ?? (Math.random() < 0.5 ? "a" : "b");

  url.pathname = `/variants/${bucket}${url.pathname}`;
  const res = await fetch(url, request);

  if (!existing) {
    const out = new Response(res.body, res);
    out.headers.append(
      "set-cookie",
      `bucket=${bucket}; Path=/; Max-Age=2592000; SameSite=Lax`,
    );
    return out;
  }
  return res;
}
```

## Edge SSR, honestly

Rendering at the edge cuts the distance to the user — but your **data** usually still lives in one region. A page that makes three database round trips from a PoP 200 ms away from the primary is *slower* than rendering in the region next to the database. Edge rendering pays off when the data is also distributed, cached at the edge, or not needed for the first paint.

The distinction to state in an interview: **the edge is close to the user; your data is not.** Move the work that needs the user (routing, auth, personalisation, headers) and leave the work that needs the data next to the data.

## Cold starts and cost

Isolates start in single-digit milliseconds, so cold start is largely a non-issue compared with container serverless. Cost is usually per request plus CPU milliseconds, which makes a cheap function on very high traffic the thing to watch — an edge function on every asset request is a bill nobody predicted.

## Key takeaways

- V8 isolates: web APIs only, tiny memory, tight CPU, no long-lived connections.
- Ideal for routing, auth gating, A/B, personalisation and headers — the request-shaped work.
- Wrong for database-heavy or compute-heavy work; that stays in a region ([SSR on Kubernetes](/system-design/114)).
- Edge SSR only wins when the data is also close.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"Edge function or serverless function?"** — Edge for request-shaped work that must be near the user; regional serverless (or a pod) when it needs a database or real CPU.
- **"How would you A/B test without a flash of the wrong variant?"** — Assign at the edge and rewrite before the response is cached, with the bucket in a cookie so it is stable.
- **"Why is your edge-rendered page slower than the regional one?"** — The data round trips. The renderer moved; the database did not.

learnings.title: Webhooks — server-to-server push, and why a browser cannot receive one
learnings.source: user paste: webhooks vs client streaming transports

summary.definition: A webhook is a reverse API call: instead of you asking a server for news, it sends an HTTP POST to a URL you registered when something happens. A browser cannot receive one, because it has no stable address for anyone to call.

api.signature: POST to a URL you registered
api.note: the whole mechanism — their server calls your server
verify it, or anyone who learns your URL can post fake events
senders time out fast and retry; do the work off the request
retries mean you will receive the same event twice — dedupe on the id
why this is server-to-server; the browser side of the same news is SSE or WebSocket
the full path when a third-party event has to reach a user's screen

summary.useCase: A payment provider confirming a charge — their server posts to yours, and your server pushes it to the waiting browser over SSE.

learnings.answer:
[WebSocket, SSE and WebTransport](/system-design/105) all answer the same question: how does a **browser** hear about a change? A webhook answers a different one: how does **another server** hear about it? Confusing the two is how a design review ends with someone asking why the browser can't just "receive a webhook".

It cannot. And the reason is the whole distinction.

## The reverse API call

![Webhooks — a reverse API call, server to server](/diagrams/sysdesign/webhook-delivery.svg)

Normally your server calls Stripe. A webhook inverts that: you register a callback URL once, and when something happens Stripe sends **you** an ordinary HTTP `POST`. No socket is held open. Between events, nothing exists.

## Why a browser can't be the receiver

A webhook requires the receiver to have a **publicly routable address that the sender can connect to**. A browser is behind NAT, a home router, a captive portal, or a corporate firewall; it has no inbound address, and nothing in the web platform gives a page a URL that another server can POST to.

Every browser transport is built the other way round: the client opens an **outbound** connection and the server pushes down it. That works from anywhere an outbound request works — which is everywhere — and it is why "the client initiates, always" is a fixed property of browser real-time, not a design choice.

So the two are not competitors. A typical system uses both:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  S["Stripe"] -->|"webhook POST"| API["Your server"]
  API --> Q["Queue"]
  Q --> W["Worker"]
  W --> DB[("DB")]
  W -->|"publish"| PS["Pub/sub"]
  PS -->|"SSE / WebSocket"| B["Browser"]
```

Stripe → your server is a webhook. Your server → the browser is SSE. The webhook is how the event enters your system; the stream is how it reaches a screen.

## Side by side

| | Webhook | WebSocket / SSE / WebTransport |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Direction | server → server | server → client (browser or app) |
| Who initiates | the **sender**, to a URL you registered | the **receiver**, outbound |
| Connection | a new short-lived HTTPS request per event | one long-lived connection |
| Public URL needed | **yes**, on the receiver | no |
| Idle cost | zero | a connection and its state, per client |
| Delivery guarantee | at-least-once, with sender-side retries | best effort; resume is your problem |
| Natural fit | Stripe payments, GitHub pushes, CI callbacks | live chat, dashboards, collaborative editing |

## Pros

**Stateless, and therefore serverless-friendly.** There is no connection to keep alive, no heartbeat, no per-client memory. The receiver can be a Lambda that is cold between events, which is impossible for anything holding a socket. Scaling is ordinary HTTP scaling — put more instances behind the load balancer.

**Delivery is the sender's problem.** Because each event is a discrete request with a status code, the sender knows whether it landed and can retry. Real providers ship an [exponential backoff](/system-design/410) ladder — Stripe retries for up to three days, GitHub gives up sooner — and park the undeliverable in a dead-letter view you can replay from. Compare with a WebSocket, where a dropped connection means the message is simply gone unless *you* built the resume cursor.

**Zero idle overhead.** A hundred thousand registered endpoints cost nothing while nothing is happening. A hundred thousand open WebSockets cost a hundred thousand sockets, whatever the traffic.

**Debuggable.** It is a `POST` with a JSON body. You can replay it with `curl`, log it, diff it, and write an integration test against it without a protocol harness.

## Cons

**Not usable from a browser.** Covered above, and the single most common reason a webhook is the wrong answer.

**Per-event overhead.** Every delivery is a fresh TCP connection and [TLS handshake](/browser/160) before any payload moves — on the order of 100ms of setup to deliver a 200-byte body. Over an already-open WebSocket that same event is a 2–14 byte frame. For occasional events this is irrelevant; for a thousand events a second it is the entire cost.

**Bursts become request storms.** A batch job that touches 50,000 records emits 50,000 webhooks, and they arrive as 50,000 concurrent HTTP requests at a receiver sized for normal traffic. Without a queue in front, the receiver falls over, starts returning 500s, and the sender's retry ladder now doubles the load on a service that is already down. Senders mitigate with per-endpoint rate limits and concurrency caps; receivers mitigate by accepting fast and processing asynchronously.

**You inherit the hard parts of a public endpoint.** It is on the internet, unauthenticated at the transport level, and anyone who finds the URL can POST to it. Signature verification is not optional.

## The receiver checklist

The part that separates "I've used webhooks" from "I've operated webhooks":

```javascript
app.post(
  "/hooks/stripe",
  express.raw({ type: "application/json" }), // raw body — see below
  async (req, res) => {
    // 1. Verify. HMAC over the RAW bytes; a re-serialised body will not match.
    let event;
    try {
      event = stripe.webhooks.constructEvent(
        req.body,
        req.headers["stripe-signature"],
        process.env.STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET,
      );
    } catch {
      return res.sendStatus(400); // do not retry-able: the signature is wrong
    }

    // 2. Dedupe. Delivery is at-least-once; you WILL see the same id twice.
    const fresh = await claimEventId(event.id); // unique index on event id
    if (!fresh) return res.sendStatus(200);

    // 3. Enqueue, don't process. Returning fast is the contract.
    await queue.publish("stripe.event", event);

    // 4. ACK.
    res.sendStatus(200);
  },
);
```

| Step | Why it exists |
| --- | --- |
| **Verify the signature** | The URL is public. Without HMAC verification anyone can fabricate a "payment succeeded". |
| **Verify over the raw body** | `JSON.parse` then `JSON.stringify` changes key order and whitespace; the HMAC no longer matches. Capture bytes before any body parser. |
| **Check the timestamp** | A signature alone permits replay of a genuine old request; reject anything older than ~5 minutes. |
| **Dedupe on the event id** | At-least-once means duplicates are normal, not a bug. A unique index is the simplest idempotency key. |
| **Return 200 fast** | Senders time out in seconds. Processing inline means a slow job turns into a timeout, a retry, and a second copy of the work. |
| **Enqueue the work** | Absorbs bursts and lets you retry *your* processing independently of the sender's retries. |
| **Tolerate out-of-order** | Retries mean `updated` can arrive before `created`. Version or timestamp your state, don't assume sequence. |

## The trace

What the retry ladder actually buys you when the receiver has a bad minute:

```trace
{
  "input": "payment_intent.succeeded (evt_9f2) while the receiver is restarting",
  "lanes": [
    { "id": "d", "label": "delivery attempts", "kind": "phases", "of": ["try 1", "try 2", "try 3", "try 4", "dead letter"] },
    { "id": "log", "label": "receiver state", "kind": "log" }
  ],
  "vars": ["sender", "receiver", "side effect"],
  "steps": [
    {
      "note": "First POST lands mid-deploy. The receiver is not accepting connections, so the sender records a failure.",
      "cursors": { "d": { "at": "try 1" } },
      "marks": { "d": { "try 1": "bad" } },
      "cells": { "log": ["connection refused"] },
      "vars": { "sender": "will retry", "receiver": "down", "side effect": "none" }
    },
    {
      "note": "Ten seconds later, attempt two. Still down — backoff widens rather than hammering a service that is already struggling.",
      "cursors": { "d": { "at": "try 2" } },
      "marks": { "d": { "try 1": "done", "try 2": "bad" } },
      "cells": { "log": ["connection refused", "connection refused"] },
      "vars": { "sender": "backoff → 2m", "receiver": "down", "side effect": "none" }
    },
    {
      "note": "Attempt three arrives after the restart. Signature verifies, `evt_9f2` is new, so it is claimed and enqueued — and the ACK goes back **before** the work runs.",
      "cursors": { "d": { "at": "try 3" } },
      "marks": { "d": { "try 2": "done", "try 3": "hit" } },
      "cells": { "log": ["connection refused", "connection refused", "200 — evt_9f2 claimed, queued"] },
      "vars": { "sender": "delivered", "receiver": "up", "side effect": "1 × fulfil order" }
    },
    {
      "note": "A duplicate arrives anyway — the sender's ACK was lost in flight, which is why delivery is at-least-once and never exactly-once.",
      "cursors": { "d": { "at": "try 4" } },
      "marks": { "d": { "try 3": "done", "try 4": "skip" } },
      "cells": { "log": ["connection refused", "connection refused", "200 — evt_9f2 claimed, queued", "200 — evt_9f2 already seen, dropped"] },
      "vars": { "sender": "delivered", "receiver": "up", "side effect": "still 1 × fulfil order" }
    },
    {
      "note": "Without the dedupe check on step 4, the customer's order ships twice. The unique index on the event id is the entire defence.",
      "marks": { "d": { "try 4": "skip", "dead letter": "skip" } },
      "cells": { "log": ["connection refused", "connection refused", "200 — evt_9f2 claimed, queued", "200 — evt_9f2 already seen, dropped"] },
      "vars": { "sender": "done", "receiver": "up", "side effect": "exactly one order" }
    }
  ],
  "result": "at-least-once delivery + idempotent receiver = effectively-once processing"
}
```

## When you are the sender

The mirror image, and a fair interview question:

- **Queue every delivery.** Emitting webhooks inline in your request path couples your latency to your slowest customer's server.
- **Sign the raw body**, and include a timestamp inside the signed payload so receivers can reject replays.
- **Retry with exponential backoff and a cap**, then dead-letter. Expose the dead letters and a manual replay button — every provider that doesn't gets support tickets instead.
- **Disable endpoints that fail persistently**, and tell the owner. Otherwise a customer who deleted their service in 2023 is still costing you retries.
- **Publish your source IPs or use mTLS**, so receivers behind a firewall can allowlist you.
- **Give the receiver an idempotency key** — a stable event id — because you cannot make delivery exactly-once, only make it safe to repeat.

## Common mistakes

- **Parsing the body before verifying.** The HMAC is over the raw bytes; re-serialisation breaks it and you end up disabling verification to "fix" it.
- **No dedupe.** At-least-once delivery plus a side effect equals double-charging someone.
- **Processing inline.** The sender times out, retries, and now the slow job runs twice concurrently.
- **Assuming order.** Retries reorder events; `updated` can land before `created`.
- **Returning 200 on a failure you swallowed.** You have told the sender it landed; it will never be sent again and the event is lost.
- **Returning 500 on a permanently bad payload.** Now it retries for three days. Reject malformed input with a 4xx.
- **Expecting a browser to receive one.** It has no address to receive it at — use SSE or a WebSocket for that hop.

## Key takeaways

- A webhook is push where the receiver has a public address; a browser stream is push where it does not.
- Each event is a standalone HTTPS request: zero idle cost, but a handshake per event and no free ordering.
- Delivery is at-least-once. Idempotency on the receiver is what turns that into correctness.
- Verify the signature over the raw body, check the timestamp, dedupe on event id, enqueue, then ACK — in that order.
- Bursts are the failure mode: accept fast, process asynchronously, or a batch job upstream becomes an outage downstream.
- Real systems use both — webhook in at the edge, SSE or WebSocket out to the screen.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"Why can't the browser receive a webhook?"** — It has no publicly routable inbound address. Browser transports are outbound-initiated for exactly that reason.
- **"How do you make webhook processing safe?"** — Treat every delivery as a possible duplicate: unique index on the event id, claim before doing work, return 200 for an already-seen id.
- **"The receiver is down for an hour. What happens?"** — The sender backs off exponentially and keeps trying for hours or days, then dead-letters for manual replay. Nothing is lost unless the ladder runs out.
- **"Webhook or polling?"** — Webhook when the receiver can expose an endpoint and events are infrequent; polling when it cannot, or when you would rather control your own load.
- **"A thousand events a second to the same endpoint?"** — That is the case where a persistent connection wins: a webhook pays a handshake per event. Batch them, or move that hop to a stream or a message bus.
