summary.useCase: An infinite feed where a new post arrives while you scroll, and offset pagination shows you the same item twice on page two.

learnings.answer:
Pagination looks like an API detail and is actually a **correctness** decision. Pick the wrong style for a list that changes while someone reads it and the bug is not slowness — it is a reader who sees the same post twice and never sees another one at all, with nothing on screen to indicate anything went wrong. ## Where offset breaks ![Pagination — offset counts positions, a cursor points at a record](/diagrams/sysdesign/pagination-styles.svg) The whole distinction in one line: **offset names a position in a list; a cursor names a record.** Positions move when the list changes. Records do not. ## The three styles | | Parameters | Fits | Costs you | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | **Offset** | `page=3&limit=20` or `offset=40&limit=20` | page numbers, jump-to-page, admin tables, search results | drifts under writes; `OFFSET 100000` makes the database read and throw away 100,000 rows | | **Cursor** | `cursor=eyJpZCI6NDJ9&limit=20` | infinite scroll, feeds, live dashboards | opaque, so no "go to page 47"; back-navigation needs you to keep the cursors you have used | | **Keyset / seek** | `published_before=&last_id=42` | chat, activity logs, [log viewers](/system-design/314), anything chronological | needs a strictly ordered, indexed key **and** a tie-breaker | Keyset is not really a fourth thing — it is a cursor whose contents are readable. That is a genuine trade: debuggable and hand-editable in a URL, at the cost of leaking your sort key and letting clients forge one. ## Drift, concretely ```trace { "input": "feed [A B C D E F G H], page size 4, offset pagination", "lanes": [ { "id": "feed", "label": "server list", "cells": ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G", "H"] }, { "id": "seen", "label": "what the reader has received", "kind": "log" } ], "vars": ["request", "returned"], "steps": [ { "note": "Page 1. Positions 1–4, and the reader starts reading.", "marks": { "feed": { "0-3": "hit" } }, "cells": { "seen": ["A B C D"] }, "vars": { "request": "offset=0 limit=4", "returned": "A B C D" } }, { "note": "While they read, someone posts **X** at the head. The list is now `[X A B C D E F G H]` — every position after the head has shifted by one.", "marks": { "feed": { "0-7": "window" } }, "cells": { "feed": ["X", "A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G"], "seen": ["A B C D"] }, "vars": { "request": "—", "returned": "list mutated under the reader" } }, { "note": "Page 2 asks for positions 5–8. Those used to be E F G H. They are now **D E F G**.", "marks": { "feed": { "4-7": "hit" } }, "cells": { "feed": ["X", "A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G"], "seen": ["A B C D"] }, "vars": { "request": "offset=4 limit=4", "returned": "D E F G" } }, { "note": "**D is rendered twice** — and H has been pushed out of the window entirely, so it is not in this page either. Neither the client nor the server has any error to report.", "marks": { "feed": { "4": "bad" } }, "cells": { "feed": ["X", "A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G"], "seen": ["A B C D", "D E F G ← D again"] }, "vars": { "request": "offset=4 limit=4", "returned": "duplicate + a gap" } }, { "note": "Now with a cursor: page 2 asks for what follows **D**. The insert of X changed no position that the query depends on, so the answer is E F G H whatever happened above it.", "marks": { "feed": { "4": "skip", "5-7": "hit" } }, "cells": { "feed": ["X", "A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G"], "seen": ["A B C D", "E F G H ✓"] }, "vars": { "request": "after=D limit=4", "returned": "E F G H" } } ], "result": "same data, same page size — the parameter decided whether the reader saw the feed correctly" } ``` A delete is the mirror image: page 2 starts one item late and something is **skipped**, which is worse because nobody notices. ## The fake cursor The sharpest question you can be asked here, and a good one to raise yourself: > Is `?cursor=startFrom34&limit=20` the same as `?offset=34&limit=20`? **Yes.** Renaming the parameter changed nothing. It still means "skip 34 rows", it still drifts when the list mutates, and the database still scans and discards 34 rows to answer it. | | `offset=34` | `cursor=startFrom34` | `cursor=eyJpZCI6MzR9` | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | The value is | a position | a position | a record | | Query | `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 34` | `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 34` | `WHERE id > 34 LIMIT 20` | | Drift under writes | yes | yes | no | | Cost at depth | O(N) — scan and discard | O(N) | O(log N) index seek | **The test, in one line:** *can the client compute the next cursor?* If `nextCursor = currentCursor + pageSize` works, it is an offset in a cursor's clothing. A real cursor is **opaque and server-minted**, because it encodes the sort key and tie-breaker it is anchored to — and the moment clients can construct one, the server can no longer change that encoding. ## The frontend half The part that is actually your job, and the part interview answers usually skip. ### Deduplicate by id, always Cursors reduce duplicates; they do not eliminate them. Retries, a [reconnect that replays](/system-design/105), and overlapping ranges all deliver the same record twice. ```javascript // Not concat. Merge by id, last write wins. function mergePage(existing, incoming) { const byId = new Map(existing.map((it) => [it.id, it])); for (const item of incoming) byId.set(item.id, item); return [...byId.values()]; } ``` This is also why the list wants [normalised state](/system-design/312): a `Map` of entities plus an array of ids, rather than pages of nested objects. React keys stay stable, a like on one screen updates every screen, and dedupe is free. ### Let the query library hold the cursors ```javascript const { data, fetchNextPage, hasNextPage } = useInfiniteQuery({ queryKey: ["feed"], queryFn: ({ pageParam }) => fetchFeed({ cursor: pageParam, limit: 20 }), initialPageParam: null, getNextPageParam: (last) => last.nextCursor ?? undefined, // The one people forget — without it, scrolling up refetches forever. getPreviousPageParam: (first) => first.prevCursor ?? undefined, }); const items = useMemo( () => mergePage([], data?.pages.flatMap((p) => p.items) ?? []), [data], ); ``` `useInfiniteQuery` (or `useSWRInfinite`) exists because accumulating pages, tracking the next cursor and keeping them cached is the same code every time. Writing it by hand is how you end up with two sources of truth for "where am I in the list". ### Bidirectional scroll anchoring Loading **older** items above the viewport must not move what the reader is looking at — the same problem as the [log viewer](/system-design/314): ```javascript // Before the prepend. const before = el.scrollHeight; await fetchPreviousPage(); // In a layout effect, before paint. el.scrollTop += el.scrollHeight - before; ``` Miss this and every "load older messages" in a chat app yanks the reader to a different part of the conversation. ### URL state, honestly Offset's real advantage is that `?page=3` is a shareable, reloadable, back-button-able URL. Cursors are not: an opaque token in a URL is meaningless tomorrow, and the back button needs the *stack* of cursors you have visited, not just the current one. Ways out, in order of how often they are the right answer: 1. **Don't sync it.** Infinite feeds mostly do not need a deep link to "page 4". 2. **Deep link the item, not the page.** `/feed?focus=post_123` is stable, meaningful and survives the list changing — which the page number never did. 3. **Keep the cursor stack in history state** (`history.pushState`) rather than the query string, so back works without an ugly URL. 4. **Keyset**, if the sort key is already public — `?before=2026-09-15T10:00:00Z` is a readable URL *and* drift-free. ## Choosing ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Does the list change
while someone reads it?"] -->|No| B["Offset is fine"] A -->|Yes| C["Does the user need
to jump to page N?"] C -->|No| D["Cursor"] C -->|Yes| E["You have a conflict —
say so out loud"] E --> F["Usually: replace paging
with search + filters"] ``` That last branch is the honest answer to "we need page numbers on a live feed": those two requirements are in tension, and the resolution is almost always that the user did not want page 47, they wanted to *find something* — which is a search problem, not a pagination one. ## Edge cases to raise unprompted - **The last page.** `nextCursor: null` is the signal; never infer "done" from a short page, because a filtered page can be short and not last. - **Empty first page** versus **end of list** — different UI, different message. - **A cursor that has been deleted.** The anchor record is gone; the server needs to fall back to the nearest valid position rather than 500. - **Sort order changes mid-session.** Every existing cursor is now meaningless — reset to the first page and say so. - **Duplicate sort keys.** Two posts at the same millisecond: without a tie-breaker, keyset silently skips one. `(timestamp, id)` is the fix. - **Refresh at the top while paginated deep.** Prepending new items must not invalidate the cursors below. ## Common mistakes - **Offset on a list that mutates.** A correctness bug, not a style preference. - **A "cursor" the client can compute.** Nothing was fixed; the parameter was renamed. - **Keyset with no tie-breaker.** Silently drops rows that share a timestamp. - **`concat` instead of merge-by-id.** Duplicate React keys and a list that grows wrong. - **Inferring the end from a short page.** Use the explicit null cursor. - **Prepending without anchoring the scroll.** The reader loses their place every time. - **Putting an opaque cursor in the URL** and calling it deep linking. ## Key takeaways - Offset counts positions; a cursor points at a record. Positions move, records do not. - Offset is correct only for data that is stable, or where drift genuinely does not matter. - Keyset is a readable cursor — debuggable, at the price of exposing the sort key and needing a tie-breaker. - If the client can compute the next cursor, it is an offset with a new name. - Dedupe by id regardless of style; cursors reduce duplicates, they do not remove them. - Cursor pagination trades away shareable page URLs — deep link to an item instead. - Prepending older content needs explicit scroll anchoring, before paint. ## Interview follow-ups - **"Why is cursor pagination better?"** — Not neater, *correct*. Offset duplicates and skips whenever the list mutates between requests. - **"Is `cursor=startFrom34` a cursor?"** — No. It encodes a position, so it drifts and still costs an O(N) scan. A real cursor is opaque and server-minted. - **"How do you support jump-to-page on a feed?"** — You mostly cannot, and I would push back: the user wants to find something, so give them search or filters rather than page numbers over shifting data. - **"Two items share a timestamp."** — Keyset needs a tie-breaker; sort and seek on `(timestamp, id)`. - **"Deep link to the fortieth post?"** — Link the post id, not the page. It stays valid when the list changes, which a page number never did. - **"You still got a duplicate with cursors. Why?"** — A retry or a reconnect replay. Dedupe by id on the client; cursors reduce duplicates but never guarantee exactly-once delivery.
